# Use AI to Draft a Simple One-Page Business Plan from Scratch in 30 Minutes

> **In short:** In about 30 minutes, you can use any major AI assistant to turn a half-formed idea into a clean one-page business plan. You supply the honest thinking about customers and money; the AI supplies the writing and layout — and it cannot read your mind on the numbers.

You don't need an MBA to write a business plan. You need an honest answer to five questions, and a writing partner that doesn't judge your typos. The AI is that partner — it does the typing, you do the thinking.

## Before you start
- A free account with any major AI assistant — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Le Chat or DeepSeek all work; the free tier is enough.
- About 30 minutes of quiet time, broken into six short tasks.
- A notes app, a Google Doc, or a piece of paper for rough thoughts you can paste into later.

## Step 1 — Describe your idea in one sentence
Open your AI assistant in a browser or app and start a new chat (look for a **"new chat"** or **"+"** button at the top — if you don't see one, just start typing, since most assistants drop you straight into a blank chat). Type a request that asks the AI to shrink your idea down to one sentence a stranger could understand. The assistant usually replies with a couple of clarifying questions (who is it for, what does it replace) and then offers a one-sentence draft. You react, it refines, and you keep going until the sentence feels right.
💬 Example: "I run a small bicycle repair shop from my garage. Help me write one sentence that explains what I do, who I do it for, and why they would pick me over a bigger shop."
You'll know it worked when you have a single sentence you could say out loud to a friend without them glazing over.

## Step 2 — Describe who your customer is
In the same chat, send the AI a follow-up message asking it to help you describe your ideal customer in one short paragraph. Include any real details you already know (a parent, a small business owner, a college student — anyone specific beats "anyone with a problem"). The assistant turns your scraps into a tidy profile with a name, a situation and a worry. If your tool has a **"regenerate"** or **"try again"** button on the reply, use it to see a second version side by side. If the first reply is too generic, push back with one short sentence: "Make this more specific — pick one real person."
💬 Example: "Based on what we just said, write one paragraph describing my ideal customer. Give them a name, a job, and one frustration that brings them to my shop."
You'll know it worked when you can picture a real person in your head, not a vague "everyone."

## Step 3 — Explain the problem and your solution
Ask the AI to write two short paragraphs: one about the problem your customer has, and one about how your offer fixes it. Tell it to keep the language plain, the way you'd say it across a kitchen table. The assistant gives you a draft in seconds; if it sounds too "marketing-y" or stuffed with adjectives, push back with a short instruction ("cut the adjectives" or "explain it like I'm 12"). If your tool offers a tone setting (formal, casual, friendly), pick **casual** or **friendly** — a business plan is not a legal document, and your reader is a human.
💬 Example: "Write two short paragraphs. Paragraph 1: the specific problem my customer has today. Paragraph 2: exactly how my bicycle repair shop solves it. Keep the language plain, like I'm talking to that customer over coffee."
You'll know it worked when a friend reading both paragraphs can repeat the problem and the solution back in their own words.

## Step 4 — Sketch the money side
Ask the AI to help you write a short section on how money flows in your business: what you sell, what you charge, and roughly how often a sale happens. You do not need real numbers yet — rough guesses written as "around $X" are honest and useful. The assistant will lay them out in a tidy list and may suggest pricing options you hadn't thought of (a monthly fee, a starter package, a yearly discount). Treat these as ideas to consider, not instructions. If the tool keeps pushing for "exact financials," tell it plainly: "Give me a simple version I can show to my partner, not an investor deck."
💬 Example: "Write a short 'How I make money' section. I charge around $40 for a standard tune-up and around $120 for a full overhaul. Customers come back twice a year on average. Help me say that in three or four sentences."
You'll know it worked when you can point to one number on the page and explain where it comes from.

## Step 5 — Ask the AI to assemble the one-pager
Ask the AI to put everything from Steps 1–4 onto a single page in this order: one-sentence idea, customer, problem, solution, money. Tell it the audience (a bank, a co-founder, your future self) and the format you want ("one page, plain English, no jargon, short sections with headers"). The assistant returns a clean draft you can copy. If your tool has a **"copy"** button at the corner of the reply, use it — then paste into Google Docs, Word, or any notes app. If the result runs longer than one printed page, tell the AI: "Cut anything that doesn't fit on one page. Keep the headers, drop the extra words."
💬 Example: "Take everything we've talked about and put it on one page in this order: my one-sentence idea, my customer, the problem, my solution, and how I make money. Use short headers, plain English, and write it for a bank loan officer who has 30 seconds."
You'll know it worked when the whole thing fits on a single page when you paste it into a document.

## Step 6 — Review, edit, and add the human touches
Read the assembled plan out loud — yes, out loud — and mark every sentence that sounds like a brochure. Replace those with the way you would actually say it. Send the edited version back to the AI for one final pass ("Tighten this. Cut filler words. Keep it warm but not salesy."). The assistant returns a cleaner version. Then add the three things only you can supply: your name, today's date, and one line about why this matters to you personally. Save the file. If your tool has a **"share"** or **"export"** button, you can use it to send the chat history to a partner — but the official one-pager is the document you just saved, not the chat log.
💬 Example: "Here's my draft one-page plan. Please tighten it: cut filler words, fix any rough sentences, keep the tone warm but not salesy. Return the final version ready to print."
You'll know it worked when you can hand the printed page to a stranger and they can explain your business back to you in one minute.

## Common mistakes
- Treating the AI's first draft as final. The fix: always read it out loud and edit. The AI gives you about 80% of the work; the last 20% is the part that sounds like you, and it's the part people remember.
- Writing for "everyone." The fix: name one specific person in your customer section. A plan that tries to serve everyone serves no one — and "everyone" never reads a one-pager twice.
- Skipping the numbers because they feel embarrassing. The fix: rough numbers written as "around $X" are honest and useful. Vague phrases like "significant revenue potential" are not — they read as a guess dressed up in a suit.
- Asking the AI to invent your financial projections. The fix: the AI can format your guesses; it cannot replace real thinking about your costs and prices. If you don't have a number yet, write "TBD" and come back to it next week.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** you'll have a one-page document you can read in 60 seconds and update any time your idea changes — much easier than a 30-page plan that gathers dust.
- **For your business or work:** you'll walk into a bank, a partner meeting, or a sleep-deprived 2 a.m. decision with a clear answer to "what am I actually doing?" — and a page you can hand over in two seconds.
- **If you're just getting started:** pick one real customer you've already talked to (or want to talk to) and write their name at the top of the page before you do anything else. That single name will keep the rest of the plan honest.

## Try it now
Open any AI assistant right now and paste this: "Help me write a one-sentence description of a business idea I have. I'll tell you the idea in my next message." Then in the next message, describe your idea in two or three rough sentences. You'll have your first sentence — and your first real plan — in under two minutes.
